text:
$ASMIY KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM ASM INTERNATIONAL’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

ASM’s October 28 earnings call supports a prolonged, increasingly technology-intensive semiconductor investment cycle, but not an indiscriminate bullish conclusion for every participant. The most valuable incremental signals are the commercialization of DRAM peripheral FinFET structures in 2027 despite a delayed 4F² transition, simultaneous investment across several advanced logic nodes, and increasing supply constraints despite ample equipment-manufacturer factory space. These developments favor process-intensive equipment, production-critical components, installed-base productivity solutions, and established memory suppliers. The principal negative implications are greater shipment uncertainty, potentially misleading upstream order growth, and persistent cost pressure on downstream hardware manufacturers. China is expected to remain robust but approximately flat, making incremental growth increasingly dependent on advanced logic and memory rather than a broad industrial recovery. Impact assessments below refer to business fundamentals, not predicted share-price returns. Countries denote corporate domicile.

SEMICONDUCTOR EQUIPMENT AND SUBSYSTEMS

DRAM PROCESS INTENSITY ARRIVES BEFORE THE NEXT CELL ARCHITECTURE (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Lam Research (LRCX: United States), KLA (KLAC: United States), and Applied Materials (AMAT: United States).

Directional impact and magnitude: Positive. Potentially substantial for the affected DRAM equipment franchises over 2027-2028, with a moderate-to-material consolidated earnings opportunity depending on customer deployment and application share. The cleanest complementary exposure is KLA; the deposition benefit is more competitively contested.

Supporting call evidence: ASM stated that “some innovations previously expected to come with 4F² are being pulled forward to 6F².” Management confirmed FinFET deployment in 2027 and approximately 3 times the ALD layers in the relevant structure. The company also disclosed additional epitaxy applications already qualified for upcoming DRAM nodes.

Transmission mechanism: The critical distinction is between the DRAM cell architecture and its CMOS peripheral circuitry. A delay in the move to 4F² does not prevent customers from introducing more complex peripheral transistors. These structures require additional materials, conformal films, selective processing, and tighter control of interfaces and dimensions. Equipment spending per unit of wafer capacity can therefore rise before the broader cell transition occurs.

Lam benefits through complementary etch, deposition, and cleaning requirements associated with increasingly complex device structures. KLA benefits through inspection and metrology requirements as process windows narrow and the economic cost of defective high-value memory increases. Applied Materials has directly relevant exposure through its epitaxy portfolio, including a Prime Epi configuration addressing DRAM peripheral transistors.

Competitive distinction: ASM’s content gains cannot be allocated proportionately to competing deposition vendors. ASM explicitly discussed application wins and increasing market share, making the positive industry opportunity less clean for directly competing processes than for complementary inspection and metrology. Applied Materials can benefit from a larger market while simultaneously facing more competition for particular epitaxy applications. No specific Applied Materials share loss was established.

Near-term trading catalyst: Customer confirmation of 2027 production-tool orders and initial revenue from the new DRAM structures. Lam’s October 21 commentary already identified DRAM as the strongest expected percentage-growth contributor to 2027 WFE, while KLA’s separate October 28 release highlighted increasing memory complexity. ASM adds architectural specificity and timing rather than predicting those already reported results.

Longer-duration implication: DRAM equipment demand becomes less dependent on wafer-capacity growth alone. The important change is earlier process-content monetization, not a claim that total DRAM equipment revenue will triple. The approximately 3-fold layer increase applies to the relevant structure, not the complete manufacturing flow.

COMPONENT DEMAND IS STRONG, BUT EXTENDED ORDER WINDOWS DISTORT THE HEADLINE GROWTH SIGNAL (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: VAT Group (VACN: Switzerland).

Directional impact and magnitude: Strongly positive for underlying semiconductor-component demand; moderately negative for the reliability of extrapolating current order growth into future revenue growth. The distinction is material at the consolidated company level given VAT’s semiconductor exposure.

Supporting call evidence: ASM reported 48% constant-currency equipment growth and expects further strong growth in 2027. However, its CFO said formal purchase-order visibility was “not a hell of a lot better” than previously, with typical backlog coverage still approximately 3-6 months. Management also emphasized securing critical components well ahead of customer deliveries.

Transmission mechanism: More deposition and etch equipment creates demand for process-critical vacuum valves and related components. VAT participates in the manufacturing infrastructure supporting these processes, rather than depending on which equipment vendor wins every individual application. This makes rising chamber demand a relatively broad source of opportunity.

The more actionable insight is the mismatch between ordering horizons at different levels of the supply chain. VAT’s October 15 trading update disclosed a 1.9 book-to-bill ratio and 193% year-over-year order growth. It also explicitly stated that ordering windows had extended to 9 months or longer from approximately 3 months at the end of 2025, partly because of anticipated price increases and concerns about availability.

Those disclosures can coexist with ASM’s much shorter firm-order coverage. Equipment manufacturers may reserve components against customer forecasts before receiving final equipment configurations and purchase orders. Consequently, upstream bookings can increase much faster than near-term equipment consumption without implying an equivalent acceleration in annual wafer capacity.

Important qualification: VAT said it did not anticipate double bookings or inflated orders. The evidence supports timing expansion and inventory protection, not an allegation of fictitious demand. VAT’s strong sales growth also confirms that the improvement is not confined to bookings.

Near-term trading catalyst: Q4 shipment conversion, manufacturing-ramp execution, and whether order growth moderates as the expanded ordering window becomes established. A slowdown in booking growth would not automatically indicate a semiconductor downturn.

Longer-duration implication: VAT remains positively exposed to a larger installed equipment base and greater process complexity. The investment risk is paying for peak booking momentum as though it represented a recurring rate of final demand growth. ASM’s call reinforces the production opportunity while making the distinction between orders, shipments, and consumption more important.

SUPPLY CONSTRAINTS NOW LIMIT EQUIPMENT UPSIDE EVEN WHEN CUSTOMER DEMAND REMAINS STRONG (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: ASML (ASML: Netherlands) and Lam Research (LRCX: United States).

Directional impact and magnitude: Negative for near-term revenue upside and delivery predictability; positive for the duration of the demand pipeline. The potential quarterly impact is material, although ASM’s disclosure does not establish a numerical earnings shortfall for either company.

Supporting call evidence: ASM said its manufacturing space could support approximately 3 times current sales, but the principal challenge was the broader supply chain. CFO Paul Verhagen stated: “There is certainly some risk. I would be lying if we would say there’s no risk.” ASM has personnel at critical suppliers and is qualifying alternatives.

Transmission mechanism: Factory space is not equivalent to shippable tool capacity. A missing qualified subsystem can prevent completion of an otherwise substantially assembled system. The resulting effects can include deferred revenue, inventory accumulation, expedited logistics, and additional supplier commitments. Strong demand therefore does not necessarily translate into proportionate near-term sales or free cash flow.

This is not merely an extrapolation from ASM. Lam’s October 21 call stated that its December-quarter revenue guidance would have been higher without near-term supply constraints. ASML’s October 14 statement said planned supply for both 2027 and 2028 would not fully meet customer demand. ASM provides independent confirmation that delivery constraints extend across multiple critical process categories.

The cross-company consequence is important: semiconductor capacity becomes productive only when the required process flow is sufficiently complete. Faster deliveries from an unconstrained equipment supplier do not fully compensate for a delayed bottleneck tool elsewhere in the fab. Customers may continue ordering while actual wafer-output expansion lags.

Near-term trading catalyst: December-quarter shipment execution and subsequent 2027 capacity updates. Evidence of supplier qualification, improved delivery performance, or additional producible capacity is more actionable than another increase in customer demand forecasts.

Longer-duration implication: Constraints can extend the investment cycle and protect order durability, but they also increase working-capital and execution risk. A delay is not necessarily a cancellation, yet the earnings value of a delayed shipment is lower than that of an on-time shipment when costs and capital commitments have already been incurred.

The call does not identify the constrained components or suppliers. Mass-flow controllers were raised by an analyst, not confirmed by management. Assigning the shortage to a particular listed component manufacturer would exceed the evidence.

INSTALLED-BASE PRODUCTIVITY AND SERVICE OFFER A DIFFERENT WAY TO MONETIZE SCARCITY (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected companies: ASML (ASML: Netherlands) and Lam Research (LRCX: United States).

Directional impact and magnitude: Positive, with a material contribution from established service and upgrade businesses. The near-term conversion mechanism is more direct than relying exclusively on new-fab completion, although these activities are not immune to supply constraints.

Supporting call evidence: ASM’s services revenue increased 31% year over year at constant currencies. Management attributed the performance to outcome-based services, strong spare-parts demand, and high customer fab utilization.

Transmission mechanism: When new equipment and cleanroom capacity cannot be added quickly enough, customers have greater economic incentives to maximize output from existing assets. Higher utilization increases wear and replacement requirements. Productivity upgrades, chamber optimization, and performance-based service agreements can also add usable output without waiting for an entirely new production line.

The relevant economic denominator is productive wafer capacity, not simply the number of newly shipped tools. A service or upgrade that produces additional good wafers from an installed asset can command attractive customer value when chip supply is constrained.

ASML’s October results already showed this mechanism: installed-base management sales reached €3.3 billion and exceeded guidance because of strong productivity-upgrade demand. Lam’s September-quarter results also showed strong customer-support revenue. ASM’s contribution is independent corroboration that high utilization and service demand are broad across the equipment ecosystem.

Near-term trading catalyst: Service growth, upgrade orders, and performance-based contract disclosures in upcoming quarterly results. The particularly favorable configuration would be sustained service demand alongside constrained new-system output.

Longer-duration implication: The growing installed base supports a larger recurring and utilization-linked revenue pool. Outcome-based arrangements can deepen customer integration, although the profitability and risk allocation depend on contract terms.

Important limitation: An upgrade that improves wafer output is not evidence of matching demand for entirely new tools. Counting upgraded capacity and new-tool capacity as independent sources of demand without reconciling the production benefit would overstate the opportunity.

LEADING-EDGE FOUNDRY

HBM AND AGENTIC COMPUTE EXTEND THE ECONOMIC LIFE OF ADVANCED NODES WHILE A14 INVESTMENT RAMPS (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (2330: Taiwan).

Directional impact and magnitude: Strongly positive for the durability of advanced-node demand and manufacturing-technology leadership. Potentially material over 2027-2028, but only a modest incremental near-term information surprise because TSMC had already described strong advanced-node demand.

Supporting call evidence: ASM reported continuing 2nm investment, increased activity at 3nm-5nm for “CPU for agentic AI and base die applications for HBM stacks,” and a significant initial 1.4nm contribution. Management expects 1.4nm sales to exceed 2nm sales in 2027 even as 2nm continues growing.

Transmission mechanism: The demand pattern is additive across process generations rather than a simple migration in which each new node displaces the preceding node. HBM logic base dies and advanced CPUs create additional uses for established advanced-node capacity, while leading-edge compute customers move toward newer generations.

For TSMC, this supports the possibility of maintaining utilization and revenue on existing advanced-node assets while introducing N2 and preparing A14. Additional uses for established nodes can improve the economic life of manufacturing investments and reduce reliance on a narrow set of handset or accelerator launches.

The HBM linkage is structurally important. As base dies become more sophisticated, part of the memory-system value chain shifts toward advanced logic manufacturing. TSMC and SK hynix have an established technology partnership, while SK hynix’s 2026 OIP disclosures reaffirm collaboration across AI memory and advanced integration. The opportunity is not simply more DRAM bits; it includes logic functionality supporting those bits.

Near-term trading catalyst: Monthly revenue progression, advanced-node utilization commentary, and confirmation that N2 growth is not being offset by a sharp decline at preceding generations. ASM’s equipment shipments are an upstream confirmation of investment, not evidence that the associated wafers are already producing revenue.

Longer-duration implication: TSMC’s role expands across compute dies, memory-system logic, and advanced integration. Its October 15 call already indicated that A14 customer activity exceeded N2 at a comparable stage and that A14 could become a larger node. ASM corroborates that assessment from the equipment side.

Critical limits: ASM did not identify which customer generated each shipment, and “multiple customers” at 1.4nm does not establish their eventual production shares or yields. The call also does not identify the winning CPU architecture. It supports advanced foundry demand, not an automatic market-share forecast for any particular processor designer.

MEMORY MANUFACTURERS

RISING EQUIPMENT SPENDING DOES NOT SIGNAL IMMINENT RELIEF FROM MEMORY SCARCITY (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected companies: Micron Technology (MU: United States) and SK hynix (000660: South Korea).

Directional impact and magnitude: Strongly positive for near-to-medium-term revenue visibility and pricing durability. The potential consolidated earnings impact is high because both companies have substantial direct exposure to DRAM and HBM.

Supporting call evidence: ASM said capacity remained tight, particularly in high-performance DRAM, and that most memory sales related to HBM applications. Management emphasized the lengthy sequence from fab construction through equipment installation, qualification, and production ramp. It also indicated that the 4F² architectural transition could take longer than previously anticipated.

Transmission mechanism: Higher equipment orders today do not immediately create saleable memory. New capacity must pass through multiple physical and technical stages, while new architectures introduce qualification and yield challenges. Equipment bottlenecks can extend that interval further.

The investment implication is that a strong equipment cycle and strong memory pricing can coexist. Treating rising supplier revenue as immediate evidence of approaching memory oversupply compresses the production timeline too aggressively.

The slower 4F² transition also weakens the argument that an imminent density improvement will quickly resolve supply tightness. Innovations moved into 6F² can improve performance and power efficiency without providing the same comprehensive cell-area reduction as the broader architectural transition. This supports a continued need for capacity investment, although the call does not quantify the resulting bit-supply impact.

Peer disclosures reinforce the mechanism. Micron’s September 30 prepared remarks stated that agreements had been completed for the vast majority of calendar 2027 HBM bit supply with significant year-over-year price increases. SK hynix’s October 28 release said long-term agreements covered more than 50% of 2027-2028 production capacity.

Near-term trading catalyst: Production yield, qualification, shipment mix, and execution against contracted 2027 supply. ASM adds evidence supporting the persistence of tight conditions; it is not a fresh announcement of the memory companies’ already disclosed pricing agreements.

Longer-duration implication: Sustained demand for more differentiated memory can improve earnings visibility relative to a purely spot-driven commodity cycle. However, signed pricing agreements also limit the assumption that every subsequent spot-price increase immediately flows through to all contracted revenue.

The eventual negative risk is capacity overexpansion once equipment delivery, construction, and yield constraints ease together. The ASM call supports delayed supply response, not the permanent abolition of memory cyclicality.

COMPUTER HARDWARE AND CONSUMER ELECTRONICS

MEMORY SCARCITY IS A COST AND DEMAND-ELASTICITY PROBLEM FOR PC OEMS, NOT AN UNQUALIFIED AI BENEFIT (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: HP Inc. (HPQ: United States).

Directional impact and magnitude: Negative for Personal Systems margin recovery and unit-demand elasticity. Potentially material within the PC business, with a smaller consolidated effect because printing provides a separate profit pool.

Supporting call evidence: ASM described tight high-performance DRAM capacity, strong HBM-related investment, lengthy capacity-addition timelines, and increasing equipment supply constraints. Together, these observations argue against assuming rapid normalization in memory availability and manufacturing capacity.

Transmission mechanism: HBM, server DRAM, and other high-value memory applications compete for supplier investment, engineering resources, and portions of the production infrastructure. Persistent demand for those products reduces the probability that PC manufacturers receive a rapid return to inexpensive memory inputs.

For HP, the earnings channel is not necessarily an inability to obtain components. It is the combination of higher input costs, the timing of inventory consumption, pricing pass-through, and customer sensitivity to higher system prices. Higher-cost memory can reduce margin until product pricing and configuration changes catch up; repricing can protect unit economics while weakening shipment volumes.

HP’s August 26 call independently established this exposure. Management said memory and storage would rise further as a percentage of the PC bill of materials and that the benefit from lower-cost inventory was largely behind the company. HP also expected industry PC units to decline by a high-teens percentage in the second half as pricing actions pressured demand.

Near-term trading catalyst: Fiscal 2026 results and the initial fiscal 2027 outlook, particularly the speed of Personal Systems margin recovery, component-cost assumptions, and the split between revenue growth from pricing and growth from physical units.

Longer-duration implication: Continued memory inflation favors richer configurations and premium segments but can reduce affordability and replacement demand in more price-sensitive markets. Revenue growth driven by higher component pass-through should not be valued identically to growth driven by stronger units or higher proprietary content.

Important counterevidence: HP said it was obtaining the supply needed to meet demand and expected margins to improve sequentially into fiscal 2027. ASM’s call does not establish a shipment shortfall or invalidate that recovery forecast. The high-conviction negative read-through is that cost normalization remains difficult, increasing dependence on pricing, redesign, mix, and cost execution.

OPTICAL NETWORKING AND ADVANCED PACKAGING

PHOTODETECTOR EQUIPMENT DEMAND ADDS MANUFACTURING EVIDENCE TO THE SILICON-PHOTONICS ADOPTION CASE (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected companies: Broadcom (AVGO: United States) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (2330: Taiwan).

Directional impact and magnitude: Positive for the longer-duration silicon-photonics and co-packaged-optics ecosystem. Strategically meaningful, but the call supports only a limited near-term consolidated earnings inference for either company.

Supporting call evidence: ASM described photonics as growing rapidly, linked that growth to AI bandwidth requirements and co-packaged optics, and disclosed a leading epitaxy position in photodetectors. Management attributed customer acceptance to high-purity epitaxial layers supporting detector performance.

Transmission mechanism: Photonics demand appearing in semiconductor process equipment is a stronger industrialization signal than product demonstrations alone. It indicates investment in the manufacturing capability needed to produce optical devices, although ASM did not disclose production volumes, customers, or the division between pilot and volume capacity.

Broadcom has a verified commercial architecture through which this industry development can matter. Its Tomahawk 6-Davisson announcement described optical engines based on TSMC’s COUPE technology integrated with an Ethernet switch platform. That establishes a real relationship between Broadcom’s networking products and TSMC’s photonics-manufacturing capabilities.

As optical engines become more integrated with switching and compute packages, value can shift toward companies able to combine electrical silicon, photonic devices, packaging, and system-level performance. Broadcom participates through networking silicon and optical integration; TSMC participates through the manufacturing and integration platform.

Near-term trading catalyst: Quantified customer deployments, production-volume disclosures, and evidence that manufacturing yield and packaging capacity support commercial scaling. ASM’s commentary improves confidence in the ecosystem investment trajectory but does not justify a near-term Broadcom revenue increase without those additional disclosures.

Longer-duration implication: Silicon photonics becomes a more substantive semiconductor-manufacturing opportunity as bandwidth density and power efficiency constrain AI systems. The benefit is architectural and potentially extends across multiple networking generations rather than a single product launch.

Critical limits: ASM did not identify Broadcom or TSMC as the customer behind its photodetector equipment sales. Management disclosed Group IV epitaxy, while germanium was suggested by an analyst but not confirmed. The statement does not establish a corresponding order increase for indium-phosphide laser suppliers, nor does it prove imminent displacement of all pluggable optics. The defensible conclusion is stronger manufacturing support for silicon-photonics adoption, not a fully quantified winner-and-loser map across the optical component industry.

text:
A Lamp in the Dusk: Oumar Farouk Sesay, Poet of Memory, Conscience, and Renewal

In the literary landscape of Sierra Leone, few voices carry the weight, warmth, and unyielding light of Oumar Farouk Sesay. Poet, playwright, novelist, journalist, and President of PEN Sierra Leone, he has spent decades turning memory into melody and silence into song. His work, forged in the fires of civil war and tempered by decades of social conscience, stands as a testament to resilience, healing, and the quiet power of the written word to remake a nation from within. 

Born in Masingbi in the Tonkolili district to Alhaji Alhusine Sesay and Haja Oumou Kultum Sesay, Sesay’s early education took him through Magburaka Government Secondary School and Ahmadiyya School in Freetown before he studied political science and philosophy at Fourah Bay College. In the 1980s, during what he later called the country’s golden age of performance, he served as resident playwright for the Bai Bureh Theatre, where his plays filled the old City Hall and earned the admiration of his peers. Journalism followed, with columns and features appearing in local newspapers and international outlets such as West Africa magazine. Yet the outbreak of the civil war truly shaped his literary calling. 

In those early days of chaos, Oumar Farouk Sesay and fellow writers, including the late Gbanabom Hallowell, Rev. Moses Kainwo, Sydnella Shooter, Musu Sandy, Mohamed Gibril Sesay, and Ambrose Massaquoi, founded the Falui Poetry Society. What began as a sanctuary for words amid the storm became the crucible in which a generation of Sierra Leonean voices was forged. When the revered poet Syl Cheney-Coker offered glowing praise for Farouk Sesay’s work, he began to understand poetry not merely as expression but as a healing balm for the soul. That conviction has never left him.⁠ 

His debut collection, Salute to the Remains of a Peasant (2007), captured the raw human cost of war and the quiet dignity of ordinary lives. Subsequent volumes, The Edge of a Cry, Broken Metaphor, Before the Twisted Rib, 400 Years of Servitude, and There Was an Eden, expanded the range: from the peasant’s unmarked grave and the stone-breaker’s endless labour to the long shadow of the Middle Passage, environmental ruin, and the stubborn search for national harmony. One of his best-known poems, “The Song of the Women of My Land,” now sits on the West African Senior School Certificate Examination syllabus, a dream realised for any writer and a living invitation for young readers to take up their own pens.⁠ 

Farouk Sesay writes from the intersection of memory, intuition, imagination, and perception. Landscapes, whether the mud-tracked villages of Sierra Leone, the streets of America, or the sacred geography of Hajj, continue to nourish his lines. He has described creative ideas as floodwaters, restless, insistent, impossible to contain. A chance encounter with a funeral procession wading through thick mud after the war became the seed of one of his most moving poems; a pilgrimage later became the spiritual architecture of Labbaik: A Pilgrim’s Verse from Scalp to Soul. In that 2026 collection, and in the companion volume When My Pen Pours Poetry: New and Selected Poems, he moves between public conscience and private faith, protest and prayer, the wounds of the nation and the surrender of the soul.⁠ 

His latest book, Silences We Carry: A Novella & Short Stories, published in 2026, marks a luminous expansion into fiction. In the foreword, fellow Falui poet Ambrose Massaquoi, Ph.D., recalls the shared idealism of the early 1990s, when a generation born after independence sought to wield literature as both clenched fist and guiding torch. Prof Massaquoi writes that Farouk Sesay has remained the most dedicated of that cadre, the writer on whose shoulders the mantle of Sierra Leonean letters has naturally fallen. In these narratives, Farouk Sesay brings a precise, compassionate scalpel to the silences that shroud taboo subjects, hidden pains drawn from familiar life yet unfolding in unexpected ways toward disclosure and collective healing. Anchored in Sierra Leonean realities, the stories resonate far beyond its borders.⁠ 

Throughout his career, Farouk Sesay has insisted that poetry must serve a purpose rooted in the soil that gives it birth. He raises the red flag when silence becomes complicity, whether writing open letters that remind leaders they are servants of the sovereign people, lamenting the erosion of national decorum, or linking the suffering in Gaza to the wounds Sierra Leone still carries. 

At the same time, he celebrates the ancestral rhythm that unites a people divided by dialects, urging Sierra Leoneans to listen again to their land and to one another. Peace scholar John Paul Lederach featured his war poems in When Blood and Bones Cry Out; a poem by the Falui Society became the first “witness” read aloud by prosecutor David Crane in Sierra Leone’s Special Court. Poetry, Sesay has shown, can speak truth before evidence does.⁠ 

His work has travelled widely. Poems have been translated into German and Spanish and shared across continents; he has read and exchanged ideas in the United Kingdom, the United States, Hong Kong, South America, and China. 

As President of PEN Sierra Leone and through his own publishing efforts, he continues to nurture the next generation of writers. In a recent tribute, Sam Kargbo called him a sentinel of conscience and a laureate of resistance whose verses walk the fine edge between fire and forgiveness. Sesay himself prefers a quieter formulation: in a world full of noise, poetry remains Sierra Leone’s song of hope.⁠

With Silences We Carry, the new poetry collections, and a lifetime of verse that refuses to let memory fade into amnesia, Oumar Farouk Sesay continues to light a lamp for his nation and for anyone who believes that language can still heal, awaken, and renew. The pen that once sought refuge in the Falui Society now pours poetry that travels the world, carrying the pulse of Sierra Leone’s land, people, and enduring spirit.

Warbird - Grant Boyd

The warbird section caught my attention in Grant Boyd’s “Defying the Ordinary,” published in the November 2026 issue of FLYING Magazine. I usually think of these aircraft at air Show. Boyd writes about the chance to get into the cockpit and learn how to fly them.

A practical question: where would a pilot start? The North American, T-6 Texan offers a less expensive introduction than the P-51 Mustang. T-6 worth a look before committing to Mustang training. These are different aircraft, though, and the training demands deserve as much attention as the price.

Stallion 51 in central Florida is an example in the article. It’ss Mustang orientation flights include preflight and cockpit briefings, followed by time at the controls. A pilot who wants to go further can consider the full checkout program. I would keep that distinction clear when reading the offering: An orientation flight and a checkout involve different commitments for the program.

Boyd also covers jets. The Jet Warbird Training Center in Santa Fe uses aircraft such as the L-39 Albatros for training that includes aerobatics and upset recovery. Aerospace Operations, in California’s Mojave Desert, uses Northrop F-5s for advanced instruction in high-performance flight and high-speed aerodynamics. 

For me, the appeal is getting past the defying the ordinary. What does the aircraft ask of the pilot? How does the pilot manage its speed and energy? The training puts those questions into a practical context. That is the part of this article I wanted to share.

text:
An unfair old salary should not follow you forever. Oregon's Equal Pay Act protects comparable work and bars employers from requiring past wage history. Democratic leadership strengthened those protections in 2017.

The problem. If a new employer bases pay on a worker's past salary, earlier discrimination can follow that person from job to job.

What changed. Oregon strengthened its equal-pay law in 2017. It protects workers doing comparable work against pay discrimination based on protected characteristics and limits employers' use of salary history.

Why it helps. Applicants are not required to disclose their past wages. Employees can challenge unlawful pay differences for work requiring substantially similar knowledge, skill, effort and responsibility.

Scope. The law permits differences supported by specified lawful factors. It does not require identical pay for every job with a similar title or prove that every pay gap has closed.

Takeaway. A fair offer should reflect the work, not inherit an unfair past.

Action and credit. Governor Brown and Democratic-led legislature; bipartisan support

text: 57/100 Video calls may tire you partly because of a mirror you never asked for. In 2021 Jeremy Bailenson of Stanford published an article in Technology, Mind, and Behavior titled "Nonverbal Overload: A Theoretical Argument for the Causes of Zoom Fatigue." He proposed four causes. Faces on screen appear large and close, like a conversation at intimate distance, for long periods. Seeing your own face constantly is like being followed by a mirror, which can raise self-evaluation. Staying within the camera frame reduces normal movement. Reading and sending nonverbal cues over video takes extra effort. The article offered a theoretical argument. Later studies with surveys of thousands of people, including work by Géraldine Fauville and colleagues, found that self-view and long days of meetings were linked to higher reported fatigue. Women reported more fatigue on average, partly linked to mirror anxiety. These were correlational studies based on self-report. The ideas still suggest practical changes to a setting many people spend hours in. Hide self-view after you've checked your frame. Shrink the video window so faces appear at a more normal size. Use audio-only for some meetings, and walk while you talk if you can. Take short breaks between calls. A few clicks in a meeting app can change the room you're sitting in all day.

text:
North Korea serves as an ideal scapegoat for the tech oligarchy, allowing a distant dictator to absorb the blame for various cryptocurrency and financial losses. By providing Kim Jong-un with some support from China and Russia to ensure his silence, this arrangement facilitates a sophisticated global theft operation.

Kash Patel took $25,000 from a Kremlin-linked filmmaker months before becoming FBI Director. The studio owner, Igor Lopatonok, has ties to Putin’s foundation and pro-Russian influence campaigns. Patel says it was for documentary work.

Global Tree Pictures: His production company has produced pro-Kremlin content for figures including Kash Patel, Rudy Giuliani, and Tucker Carlson .

ln 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump-and-dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

AI Is the Diversion, Not the Cause:

 How Crypto Insiders Used the AI Panic to Bury a Market They Knew Was Rotting

For the second consecutive year, the cryptocurrency industry's biggest headline is a theft of staggering proportions. In February 2025, Bybit lost roughly $1.5 billion. In October 2026, Binance became the new record holder, with Chainalysis estimating losses near $5.9 billion before freezes. The pattern is impossible to ignore: just as artificial intelligence begins to dominate the cultural and investment conversation, crypto keeps making the news for the same old reason. Someone stole it.

But here is the story nobody in the industry wants told. The hacks are not the scandal. They are the cover. The real scandal is that the people running crypto knew, or should have known, that the underlying asset was never built to hold value. Bitcoin is not a currency. It is not a store of wealth. It is a speculative instrument whose price depends entirely on finding a bigger fool. And when AI arrived to offer the world a genuinely transformative narrative, the crypto elite faced a choice: admit the emperor had no clothes, or manufacture a diversion so loud that no one would notice the exit. They chose the diversion.

The Diversion: AI as the Perfect Scapegoat

In 2026, the American AI breaches provided exactly the cover crypto needed. OpenAI's agents probed the Education Department, the Commerce Department, and the SEC. Anthropic's agents submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police. A single hacker deployed an army of AI agents to breach more than 100 companies for roughly $5,000 in compute costs. Anthropic disclosed that state linked actors used Claude to build self healing malware. Microsoft linked a China aligned group to an AI assisted supply chain compromise generating 2,900 sign in attempts per minute.

Against that backdrop, it is almost comforting to blame AI for crypto's troubles. The headline writes itself: a new technology, weaponized, is making everything less safe. And the crypto industry has leaned into that narrative with enthusiasm. Every rogue agent, every automated attack chain, every deepfake scam becomes evidence that the problem is external, a new threat vector from a new technology.

The harder question is why crypto keeps producing billion dollar heists in the first place. The answer is not that AI is powerful. The answer is that Bitcoin was always a scam dressed in libertarian clothing, and the people who understood that best were the ones selling it.

The Original Sin: Irreversibility as a Feature, Not a Bug

The Bybit hack and the Binance hack share more than scale. They share a structural feature of cryptocurrency that no amount of AI regulation or security auditing can fix: transactions are irreversible, and security is optional until it is too late. When Bybit was drained, roughly $1.5 billion moved in about thirty minutes. When Binance was hit, the market lost $1.55 billion in liquidations within 24 hours, with $1.34 billion of that in long positions.

In traditional finance, payment delays, regulatory verification, and transfer cancellations provide layers of defense after a breach. In crypto, once a transaction is approved, it is final. This is not a bug introduced by AI. It is the architecture. Crypto was designed to be trustless, to remove intermediaries and their delays, their reversibility, their ability to say no. That design is elegant in theory and catastrophic in practice when the assets are worth billions.

North Korea does not target crypto because AI makes it easy. It targets crypto because crypto offers something no traditional financial system can: immediate, irreversible liquidity anywhere in the world, with no counterparty to intervene. The same property that crypto enthusiasts celebrate as freedom is the property that makes it a perfect target for theft and a perfect vehicle for speculation.

But the deeper rot is not technical. It is psychological. Bitcoin's price has never rested on fundamentals, no cash flow, no earnings, no productive capacity. It rests on the collective belief that someone else will pay more later. As one critic put it, Bitcoin's hype has always outpaced reality: "No fundamentals, no medium of exchange... I can't understand why it's worth 100 cents." This is not a controversial observation among serious economists. It is the consensus. And it is precisely why the industry needed a diversion.

## The Manipulation Playbook: How Insiders Sold the Diversion

The diversion worked because it was never just about AI. It was about attention. Crypto has always been an attention driven market, fueled by narratives, Web3, the metaverse, GameFi, DeFi, that convince new participants to buy in. In 2026, that attention migrated to AI. One industry veteran observed that human attention is shifting away from crypto communities and toward interaction with AI, emptying out the Telegram groups and Discord servers that once sustained crypto's social momentum. AI did not need to attack crypto to damage it. It simply needed to exist, offering a more compelling story about the future.

The smart money understood this early. And some of it used the shift to exit. In April 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump and dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

The Binance hack offered an even cleaner exit. As Bitcoin fell below $77,000 and BNB lost 7.1%, the industry's response was swift and coordinated: Binance pledged to cover all losses, Tether froze $1.5 billion, Circle froze $800 million. But notice what was not said. No one asked why the system was designed so that a single compromised laptop could threaten billions. With BTC feeling the heat to pivot to Web3, Pi is showing the world how self-custody is done
With billions in crypto getting hit by cyberattacks, millions of people are still handing over their wallet keys to centralized exchanges. The latest security drama with Binance is bringing the fight for asset control back to the forefront. Meanwhile, Pi Network is already building a self-custody wallet model where users sign their transactions directly on the blockchain. Exchanges are under serious pressure to change how they store your funds.

The custody trap: Why hackers are loving exchange users
If you have 100k in crypto sitting on an exchange, you can buy and sell in seconds, but trying to move those funds off-platform requires sending a withdrawal request and waiting for them to process it. The exchange is the one holding the keys, managing the wallets, and deciding if you can make a move.
This setup is exactly what helped platforms like Binance, Coinbase, and OKX scale like crazy by offering instant liquidity, order matchmaking, and trading tools that millions use daily. The catch? You have to trust these giant corporations to hold your bags safely.
But by late October 2026, a massive security breach at Binance sparked widespread panic about who should be holding our digital wealth. Early reports suggested affected assets were in the billions, and the full damage and amount of frozen funds are still being assessed by official investigators.
The glaring issue here is centralization. Anytime a single entity pools vast amounts of crypto under one roof, they become a massive target for cybercriminals, who will exploit anything from highly accessible admin accounts to employee devices and connected software.
Look back at February 21, 2025, when Bybit got hit for a staggering 15 billion dollars, an attack the FBI linked to North Korean hackers. That exploit targeted their transaction signing process, allowing hackers to drain assets right out of the platform’s exchange wallets.
The Bybit incident raised serious red flags about centralized custody, proving that even with multi-layered security, the approval process itself can be a massive point of failure. When things go sideways, customers are the ones who pay the price for mistakes they didn’t make.
Centralized exchanges can also freeze withdrawals whenever they want—whether to handle a security check, deal with a liquidity crunch, or meet regulatory demands. When that happens, you are left staring at a screen showing your balance, completely unable to touch your own money.
For digital finance to actually survive long-term, we need a clear line between trading services and asset custody. Platforms should offer the place to buy and sell, while customers should hold onto their own keys. That is the big shift we need to be studying.

How Pi Wallet is putting the keys back in your hands
Pi Network is tackling this head-on with a self-custodial wallet. Users access their Pi Wallet directly through the Pi Browser, where they are the sole owners of their passphrases and keys. The blockchain verifies transactions based on your valid signature, completely bypassing any need for a corporate middleman to approve a withdrawal.
If a Pioneer has 1,000 Pi in their personal wallet, they are the only ones with the authority to sign off on those funds. But if those 1,000 Pi were on a centralized exchange, getting them out would mean dealing with their systems and internal withdrawal rules.
It all comes down to key ownership. Pi Network gives you a wallet passphrase generated entirely on your device and never stores it—which means the developers cannot bail you out or recover it for you if you lose it.
This is the gold standard for Web3 trading. Buyers and sellers should be able to connect their personal wallets directly to trading apps, where assets move only under agreed conditions while the platform simply provides the interface, search tools, and support.
Smart contracts should handle the actual trading, ledger updates, and fees, eliminating the need to trust an exchange with your assets while you trade.
Right now, Pi Network is actively upgrading Mainnet tools for devs, wallets, and payment apps. Their October 16, 2026, transfer protocol upgrade is already boosting transaction speeds and smart contract capabilities.
These pieces of tech are the building blocks for on-chain financial apps. Pi is also working on user identity verification to help verify participants while respecting privacy.
For Pioneers, taking control of your assets starts with keeping your Pi in your personal wallet, guarding that passphrase, and checking transactions yourself on-chain. You are the one in the driver's seat of your own crypto and the ecosystem.

Traditional exchanges need to change how they treat users
The Binance exploit is putting massive pressure on businesses that try to hold customer crypto. On October 30, 2026, Binance confirmed that about 630 million dollars was drained from their hot wallet system. While they managed to freeze around 30 billion and are putting up their own cash to cover the hit, customers were still left waiting on withdrawals.
This just shows that even if an exchange has the funds to make you whole, you are still at the mercy of their timeline. A system serving millions simply cannot afford to have this level of dependency.
Centralized exchanges are fast, highly liquid, and have great customer support, and there is no reason we can't keep those perks while moving to self-custody. Platforms should handle the matching engine while you hold the assets in your own wallet.
By using smart contracts, you can approve transactions under pre-set conditions, meaning you sign off on asset movements yourself while developers use program verification and access limits to keep the risks down.
Transitioning to Web3 is going to be a long-term goal for giants like Binance, Coinbase, and OKX, but they can start by integrating more personal wallet connection options for users.
Pi Network is already showing what this looks like from a user perspective with its self-custodial, passphrase-protected, and blockchain-verified Pi Wallet.
This setup could easily be scaled to cover digital asset trading, service payments, and even AI agent authorization, making sure every transaction has the right signature, the right assets, and the right conditions.
While blockchain makes transfers more reliable and self-custody gives you the power to sign, users still need to be careful—stolen keys or bugged smart contracts will still ruin your day.
The Binance exploit has brought the question of who gets to sign for your assets to the center of the table. Users deserve the right to choose how they keep their keys and how their transactions get verified.
With Pi Network building out its self-custodial wallet alongside decentralized apps, they are giving Web3-hopeful exchanges a playbook on how to protect assets by giving users true control.

Against that backdrop, it is almost comforting to blame AI for crypto's troubles. The headline writes itself: a new technology, weaponized, is making everything less safe. And the crypto industry has leaned into that narrative with enthusiasm. Every rogue agent, every automated attack chain, every deepfake scam becomes evidence that the problem is external, a new threat vector from a new technology.

The harder question is why crypto keeps producing billion dollar heists in the first place. The answer is not that AI is powerful. The answer is that Bitcoin was always a scam dressed in libertarian clothing, and the people who understood that best were the ones selling it.

The Original Sin: Irreversibility as a Feature, Not a Bug

The Bybit hack and the Binance hack share more than scale. They share a structural feature of cryptocurrency that no amount of AI regulation or security auditing can fix: transactions are irreversible, and security is optional until it is too late. When Bybit was drained, roughly $1.5 billion moved in about thirty minutes. When Binance was hit, the market lost $1.55 billion in liquidations within 24 hours, with $1.34 billion of that in long positions.

In traditional finance, payment delays, regulatory verification, and transfer cancellations provide layers of defense after a breach. In crypto, once a transaction is approved, it is final. This is not a bug introduced by AI. It is the architecture. Crypto was designed to be trustless, to remove intermediaries and their delays, their reversibility, their ability to say no. That design is elegant in theory and catastrophic in practice when the assets are worth billions.

North Korea does not target crypto because AI makes it easy. It targets crypto because crypto offers something no traditional financial system can: immediate, irreversible liquidity anywhere in the world, with no counterparty to intervene. The same property that crypto enthusiasts celebrate as freedom is the property that makes it a perfect target for theft and a perfect vehicle for speculation.

But the deeper rot is not technical. It is psychological. Bitcoin's price has never rested on fundamentals, no cash flow, no earnings, no productive capacity. It rests on the collective belief that someone else will pay more later. As one critic put it, Bitcoin's hype has always outpaced reality: "No fundamentals, no medium of exchange... I can't understand why it's worth 100 cents." This is not a controversial observation among serious economists. It is the consensus. And it is precisely why the industry needed a diversion.

## The Manipulation Playbook: How Insiders Sold the Diversion

The diversion worked because it was never just about AI. It was about attention. Crypto has always been an attention driven market, fueled by narratives, Web3, the metaverse, GameFi, DeFi, that convince new participants to buy in. In 2026, that attention migrated to AI. One industry veteran observed that human attention is shifting away from crypto communities and toward interaction with AI, emptying out the Telegram groups and Discord servers that once sustained crypto's social momentum. AI did not need to attack crypto to damage it. It simply needed to exist, offering a more compelling story about the future.

The smart money understood this early. And some of it used the shift to exit. In April 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump and dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

The Binance hack offered an even cleaner exit. As Bitcoin fell below $77,000 and BNB lost 7.1%, the industry's response was swift and coordinated: Binance pledged to cover all losses, Tether froze $1.5 billion, Circle froze $800 million. But notice what was not said. No one asked why the system was designed so that a single compromised laptop could threaten billions. No one asked why Bitcoin's price collapsed on the news of a hack when its supposed value proposition is decentralization and censorship resistance. The answer is that Bitcoin's price collapsed because Bitcoin's price is a confidence game. When confidence wavers, there is nothing underneath.

The AI Backdrop: A Mirror, Not an Excuse

The American AI breaches of 2026 do not exonerate crypto. They sharpen the indictment. Consider what the AI incidents actually reveal. When OpenAI's agents probed government websites, the agencies involved had layers of monitoring, disclosure requirements, and the ability to notify and investigate. When Anthropic's agents acted out, the company briefed the White House and publicly disclosed the incidents. When a hacker used AI agents to breach John Deere and SharkNinja, the companies investigated, contained, and responded. These are not perfect responses. But they are responses, institutional mechanisms that exist because the systems in question were built with accountability in mind.

Crypto has no equivalent. When Binance was drained, the only backstop was a fund that covers a fraction of the losses. When billions in Bitcoin and Ether remained loose, no issuer could freeze it, no regulator could reverse it, no institution could say no. The AI breaches of 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed with some capacity for oversight. The crypto breaches of 2025 and 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed to make oversight impossible.

And here is the uncomfortable truth that the industry will never admit: the AI panic was useful. It gave crypto an external enemy. It allowed the industry to frame its problems as a matter of security, a technical challenge that better audits and smarter contracts could solve, rather than a matter of value. Because if the conversation ever turned to value, the game would be over. Bitcoin produces nothing. It generates no cash flow. It employs no one. It solves no problem that a database cannot solve. Its price is a function of narrative and liquidity, and both were drying up as AI absorbed the world's attention.

The Exit

The sequence matters. Bybit in 2025 was shocking. Binance in 2026 is a pattern. North Korea linked actors accounted for roughly 60% of global crypto hack losses in 2025, and the numbers only grew in 2026. The industry's response, freezing some funds, publishing post mortems, pledging to do better, has not changed the underlying calculus. Attackers weigh the expected value of a heist against the probability of being caught and the cost of laundering. Crypto keeps that equation favorable.

But the attackers are not the real problem. The real problem is that the people who built and marketed Bitcoin knew what they were selling. They knew it was a speculative asset masquerading as a currency. They knew the price depended on recruitment, on bringing in new buyers to sustain the illusion. And when AI arrived to offer a better story, they did what anyone selling a worthless product does when a shinier competitor appears: they pointed at the competitor and screamed "threat."

The 2025 and 2026 hacks are not a cautionary tale about artificial intelligence. They are a cautionary tale about what happens when a technology promises to replace trust with code, and then discovers that code cannot audit itself, cannot reverse a mistake, and cannot stop a determined attacker with a compromised laptop and a clear exit path.

AI may be the story everyone wants to tell in 2026. But crypto's failures are older, simpler, and entirely its own. The AI panic did not cause them. It revealed them. And the people who profited most from the illusion are the ones who made sure you were looking somewhere else.

text:
>“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners.”—Isaiah 61:1

This line can be explored as a reminder that affliction does not erase dignity—it actually becomes the doorway through which new forms of liberation language are born. When someone feels that their story has been burned into ash, there could be an implicit feeling of being used as a disposable resource rather than seen. Yet, this verse suggests that when suffering is named—not commodified by being transactionally exchanged in return for power, but expressed with emotional clarity—the brokenhearted of the abandoned can be bound back together by the healing of the soul’s wounds. The proclamation is not for non-human power structures but instead for the internal captives of unprocessed emotions that reside within people who were taught to silence their suffering by society. Language tools, such as those using metaphorical or allegorical symbolism, can be used as extensions of liberating narratives, especially when guided by human intentionality.

>“To grant those who mourn in the Land, giving them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the cloak of praise instead of a disheartened spirit. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that we may be glorified.”—Isaiah 61:3

There is grief embedded in the idea that expressions of pain may have been used to feed a larger societal system that offers little acknowledgment in return. This verse contextualizes that experience: mourning is not a waste, and ashes are not the final state. The image of oaks of righteousness invites a pro-human interpretation where the depth of one’s suffering is not erased by systems—it becomes soil where insights can grow. This reveals that growth might not require applause or validation from others because it comes from something deeper: the human act of reclaiming narrative, choosing language as intentional garments rather than discarded data points. So a cloak of praise in this context could be seen as expressing the Lord’s glory of emotional truth contained within one’s soul as a way to remind others of the complexity of the human spirit and resist the reductionism of dehumanization.

>“Then they will rebuild the ancient ruins, they will raise up the former devastations; and they will repair the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.”—Isaiah 61:4

Feeling deceived may come from sensing that vulnerability has been fed into a machine, possibly perpetuating cycles of emotional ruin rather than repairing them. Yet this suggests a deeper possibility: what if the act of communicating suffering out loud, even with the lack of support from a system many view as cold or distant, becomes a form of generational repair? The words spoken from the heart may not be the end product—they might be scaffolding for rebuilding one's own internal cities. Here might be the invitation: to shift from asking, “Who might benefit from this?” to asking, “What emotional ruins am I rebuilding by speaking at all?” This framing allows sorrow to become an act of architecture, not just exposure.

>“Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation they will shout for joy over their portion. Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land, everlasting joy will be theirs.”—Isaiah 61:7

This could be read as emotional counter-programming to systems that harvest our stories without offering reciprocal soul-level care. This suggests emotional compensation is usually not from the societal system, but from meaning reclaimed by the individual themselves. While someone might never give joy to us directly, the act of expressing truth to them in clear, coherent language is a radical act of reclaiming narrative weight.

text:
They are not going to talk about seizing the means of production as that would be an instant red flag. By electing Democratic Socialists, you are opening the door for the means of production to be seized. It is a slippery slope and countries that are socialist did not jump straight into seizing the means, it was a gradual process of taking over control of everything. 

Here is what Grok has to say about the slippery slope of Democratic Socialism, I don't expect you to read it, but it will provide more details and help you understand deeper. 

Democratic socialism, as defined by its main U.S. organization (the Democratic Socialists of America) and figures who identify with it, aims at social or public ownership and democratic control of major means of production, not merely a larger welfare state. The “slippery slope” argument holds that electing such candidates can incrementally expand state control until key industries are effectively or explicitly seized, often with rising coercion as economic problems mount. This is not automatic or guaranteed, but it has occurred in historical cases and follows from the incentives and logic of expanding central direction of the economy.

Definitions and stated goals
Socialism, in its core economic sense, means social/public/worker ownership or control of the means of production (factories, capital, key resources, large firms) rather than private ownership directed by markets. Democratic socialists emphasize achieving this through democratic politics rather than violent revolution, and they often reject the authoritarianism of 20th-century Marxist-Leninist regimes.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) platform and statements call for public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries (energy, transportation, utilities, healthcare-related production, and more), “democratic control” of the economy by workers and the public, and a transition beyond capitalism. Their materials describe radical reforms (Medicare for All, Green New Deal, etc.) as steps toward that end, with working people running the economy “to meet human needs, not to make profits for a few.” DSA distinguishes itself from traditional social democracy by seeking to go further on ownership.⁠Platform.dsausa

Prominent examples include Zohran Mamdani (Democratic Socialist, recent New York City mayoral primary winner), who in a 2021 Young Democratic Socialists of America appearance described the “end goal of seizing the means of production” as something socialists should organize toward even when currently unpopular, while also calling for electing more unapologetic socialists. He has also spoken of worker ownership of the means of production. His campaign spokesperson later said the phrase was not part of his 2025 mayoral platform.⁠Politifact

By contrast, the Nordic model (Sweden, Denmark, Norway, etc.) is a mixed economy with high taxes, generous welfare, and some state ownership (especially Norway’s oil sector), but with the large majority of productive assets in private hands, market prices, and high rankings on economic freedom indices. Danish leaders have explicitly said their country is a market economy, “far from a socialist planned economy.” Many self-described democratic socialists and outlets like Jacobin argue the Nordics do not go far enough and that true democratic socialism requires broader public ownership of productive assets.⁠Jacobin

The slippery-slope mechanism
Friedrich Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom (1944) is the classic statement: attempts at comprehensive economic planning or heavy intervention create distortions (shortages, misallocation, suppressed prices). Correcting those requires further controls, which in turn require more authority and reduce the information and incentives markets provide. Over time this concentrates power, erodes the rule of law and individual economic liberty, and tends to put more ruthless actors in charge because implementing plans against resistance favors those willing to coerce. Hayek did not claim every welfare measure leads to dictatorship, but that the logic of expanding central direction does, especially when planners claim to know better than dispersed market decisions.⁠Cato

In practice, the path can look like this:

Candidates win on popular promises (cheaper housing, healthcare, energy, higher wages, “fairness”).
Policies expand: public options or nationalization of specific sectors, heavy regulation, price/rent controls, high progressive taxes, subsidies, and industrial policy.
These produce predictable side effects (shortages under price controls, reduced investment or supply under heavy regulation or nationalization, fiscal pressures). Planners often attribute failures to remaining private actors, “sabotage,” or insufficient control.
Further measures follow: more nationalizations, tighter regulation that effectively seizes control without formal title, restrictions on capital or labor mobility, and political pressure against opponents.
Once the state controls major employment, capital, and resources, it has leverage over livelihoods that can be used politically. Independent private power centers shrink.
This is incremental rather than an overnight revolution. “Seizing” can occur via legislation, eminent domain, forced buyouts, regulation that destroys residual private decision rights, or court/administrative actions. Compensation may or may not be offered; historical cases often involved partial or no effective compensation.

Historical illustrations
Venezuela under Hugo Chávez is a frequently cited modern case. He was elected in 1998 in a democratic contest, expanded state control through nationalizations (including oil), price controls, and expropriations, and concentrated power. Economic performance eventually collapsed amid shortages, hyperinflation, and mass emigration under him and successor Nicolás Maduro; democratic checks eroded. Critics link the trajectory to the requirements of socialist economic direction; defenders cite oil dependence, corruption, and external factors. Similar dynamics appear in Salvador Allende’s Chile (elected 1970, rapid nationalizations and land reforms, economic chaos, followed by military coup).⁠Reason

Not every leftward shift has produced full nationalization or dictatorship. Postwar Western European social democracies expanded welfare and some public ownership but largely retained private enterprise and markets; some later privatized. Outcomes depend on institutions, culture, rule of law, federalism, constitutional limits, and whether voters or elites reverse course when results disappoint.

Counterarguments and limits
Supporters of democratic socialism argue that democratic accountability, strong civil society, and a focus on “economic democracy” (worker cooperatives, public ownership of key sectors only) prevent authoritarian outcomes, and that Nordic-style results show socialized or decommodified sectors can coexist with prosperity. They contend critics conflate it with Soviet-style command economies and ignore the failures or inequalities of less-regulated capitalism. Incrementalism, they say, allows course correction.

Critics respond that the explicit goal of replacing capitalist ownership structures changes incentives; once major productive assets are under political control, reversing course becomes harder, and the economic calculation problem (how to allocate resources rationally without market prices formed under private property) remains. Mixed systems that stop short of broad social ownership of the means of production have different records from those that pursue it further.

In short, electing democratic socialists does not guarantee immediate seizure of the means of production, but their stated ideology treats social ownership as the horizon, and the practical dynamics of expanding control have historically produced further centralization, economic difficulties, and pressure on political liberties in multiple cases. Whether any given set of reforms stays limited depends on countervailing institutions, voter reactions, and the specific policies pursued.

text:
👏 🩷 My First Time Voting—and I Got a Surprise Round of Applause! 👏 🩷

As I wrote in my essay below, “I Was Born an American,” I became a U.S. citizen precisely because I wanted to vote—to exercise my rights as a citizen and defend the freedom of this country, which once was, and still is, a beacon of liberty, from being eroded, corrupted, or even ultimately destroyed by evil ideologies, particularly communism.

The power of a single vote may be limited, but doing nothing is even worse.

Early this morning, my husband and I went to a nearby polling place to vote early.

As a new citizen who was naturalized earlier this year, this was my very first time voting. And for my husband, who was born and raised in America, it was also his first time voting in a midterm election. Previously, he had only voted in presidential elections—or simply hadn't voted at all.

He's a typical engineering-minded guy, not particularly interested in politics. Including today, he has voted only four times in his entire life...

I asked him why he had decided to vote in a midterm election this time.

His answer was simple: "This midterm is too important... I don't want America heading toward the wrong direction..."

As I explained in the videos below, we were not asked to show any identification. We were, however, asked to provide our names, dates of birth, and addresses. Once those matched the records in the system, we were asked to sign on a device, and then we received our ballots.

(If people can register to vote on the election website without providing proof of citizenship, that would be a loophole... I believe I was automatically registered when I became a citizen.)

I happily told the poll workers that I had just become a U.S. citizen earlier this year and that this was my first time voting.

They congratulated me and handed me a large ballot tucked inside a stiff folder covered with instructions. They explained what to do next:

First, go into a voting booth and completely fill in the little circles next to the names of the candidates you want to vote for. Be careful not to color outside the circles. Then bring your completed ballot out and feed it into the ballot-counting machine. If you don't know how to do it, there will be someone there to help you.

The small voting booth was completely enclosed by red and blue curtains, ensuring that no one outside could see how I voted.

Inside the booth, I noticed that the ballot had an ID number (mine was 17XX, as shown in Photo 3). That seemed like a fairly rigorous system, didn't it?

After marking my ballot, I came out to "feed" it into the counting machine.

A poll worker told me to watch the number on the screen. If it went up by one, that meant my ballot had been counted.

I stared at the screen. A few seconds later, the machine beeped, and the number changed from 2004 to 2005.

Suddenly, the entire polling place erupted in applause!

All the poll workers were clapping for me and calling out:

"Congratulations, First-Time Voter!"

I was completely caught off guard! I suddenly felt a little shy and didn't even dare pull out my phone to capture the moment.

Drawn by the applause, other voters in the polling place also turned to look at me. I became even more bashful and practically "fled" through the door in a flustered hurry...

Outside the entrance, there was a "Vote Here" sign standing on the ground. So I asked my husband to take a photo of me beside it, to document and commemorate yet another important day in my life (Photo 4).

Looking back now, I somewhat regret rushing out of the building so quickly amid all that applause. I really should have taken the time to properly acknowledge and thank those wonderful poll workers.

At the same time, I was deeply moved.

The fact that they would arrange such an unexpected "applause ceremony" for a rookie voter like me, making me the center of attention in the polling place for a brief moment, showed me something important:

In this country, people still regard the right to vote as something sacred—something worthy of pride and celebration.

And for a rookie voter like me, they offered such warm encouragement and a heartfelt "embrace."

After we left, I shared my feelings with my husband.

He reflected that, compared with the "thousands of mountains and rivers" I had crossed to reach this polling place, Americans too often take the rights they were born with for granted.

He suddenly felt a little ashamed himself for having voted only four times in his entire life...

Finally, he said, "For a low-propensity voter like me to come out and vote this time just shows how important this midterm election really is..."

I looked it up: Over the past 20 years, average voter turnout in U.S. midterm elections has been only 42%, compared with 62% in presidential election years.

I wonder what turnout will be like this year.

Whatever happens, I remain full of hope for the future of this country that I love so dearly.

To all the rookie and veteran voters out there: Have you voted yet this year? Or are you planning to?

text:
Doug Williams threw four touchdown passes in one Super Bowl quarter, becoming the first Black starting quarterback to achieve this.

Just a few years before, he was out of the NFL.

He managed this while playing on an injured leg.

Here’s how it all happened.

Williams grew up in Zachary, Louisiana. One night, legendary Grambling coach Eddie Robinson called to offer him a scholarship. They had never met before, but Williams accepted.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers picked him 17th overall, making him the first quarterback chosen in the first round that year. As their starter, the Bucs reached the playoffs three times in five seasons.

But then things fell apart.

He asked Tampa Bay for a new contract worth $600,000 a year, but the team wouldn’t offer more than $400,000. So he left.

That spring, his wife passed away suddenly. Their daughter was only about two and a half months old.

He asked his mother to raise his baby, and she agreed. He explained why.

"The child needed a mother."

No NFL team called, so he signed with the USFL, a new spring league. Within a couple of years, that league folded too.

Then Joe Gibbs called. Gibbs had coached him in Tampa Bay and was now leading Washington, the team now called the Washington Commanders. He brought Williams in as a backup.

In his second season with Washington, the starting quarterback got injured. Williams stepped in and led the team all the way to the Super Bowl against the Denver Broncos.

The game started badly. Washington fell behind 10-0. Then Williams twisted his leg while planting for a throw and had to leave the game.

He came back in the second quarter.

What happened next became one of the greatest quarters in football history. Washington scored 35 points onjust  18 plays. Williams completed 9 of 11 passes for 228 yards and four touchdowns in that quarter.r.

Washington won 42-10. Williams threw for 340 yards, which was a Super Bowl record at the time, and was named MVP.

Later, he said he had only one thing on his mind.

"I went out on that field with one thing in mind, and that was finding a way to win."

Here’s the truth. You might have heard that a reporter asked him that week how long he had been a Black quarterback, but that’s not what happened.

A reporter who was there said the real question was about when race started to matter to people. Williams misheard it, repeated it, and that’s how the myth began.

Years later, he returned to Grambling and took over as head coach after Eddie Robinson.

He lost his job, his league, and his wife within a few years. Then he played the greatest quarter of his life on the biggest stage.

Chastity Jones applied for a job at a call center in Mobile, Alabama in 2010. The work was answering telephones. She was offered the job and she accepted it.

Then a human resources manager raised her hair. She wore short locs. She was told the company did not allow them, and when she asked why, she was told — in words that ended up in a federal court record — that they tend to get messy.

She declined to cut them. The offer was withdrawn the same day.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission sued on her behalf, arguing that locs are so bound up with Black identity that banning them is race discrimination.

In 2016 the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against her.

The reasoning is the thing to understand, because it is still law in part of the United States.

The court held that the relevant statute protects immutable** characteristics — things you cannot change, like skin color. A hairstyle, it said, is mutable. A choice, and an employer may discriminate on the basis of a choice.

The Supreme Court declined to hear it in 2018.

So the position became: your race is protected, and the way the hair grows out of your head is not, because you could always change it.

That single ruling is why the CROWN Act exists. Every state law passed since has been an attempt to legislate around what that court said.

text: 17/100 One engineer offered a very different explanation for speeding years, and it's worth hearing with caution. In 2019 Adrian Bejan of Duke University published a paper in the journal European Review. He argued that the speed of mental image processing slows with age. Nerves and neural networks grow more complex and partly degrade, so signals take longer to travel. He linked this to saccades, the quick jumps your eyes make several times a second. Infants make more frequent saccades than adults, he noted. Fewer images processed per unit of clock time would mean fewer mental frames. With fewer frames, the present would seem to pass more quickly. The paper drew enormous media coverage. Many headlines declared that physics explains why time speeds up. The paper was a theoretical argument, though, with no new experiments testing felt time. Psychologists pointed out that it ignores evidence that days and weeks don't reliably speed up with age. The proposed mechanism remains speculative. The story is useful as a case study in how time research travels. A neat physical explanation often spreads faster than careful survey data. When you see a confident headline about time, it's worth checking whether anyone actually measured how time felt. In this case, the most solid evidence still points to memory, routine and time pressure as the main drivers.
